title: A Brief History of Islamic Education in Singapore
subtitle: Rooted in Tradition. Shaped by Singapore.
introduction: Islamic education in Singapore has grown through generations of scholars, educators, philanthropists and institutions. Rooted in Islamic traditions and the local socio-religious context, it is enriched by scholarly networks across the Malay world and beyond.
This exhibition traces selected milestones from the 19th to the 21st century, highlighting a cosmopolitan and adaptive tradition.
Selected texts and manuscripts showcase Singapore’s Islamic intellectual heritage and SCIS’s commitment to its preservation and study through research and the Library’s Special Collections.
SCIS continues this intellectual legacy and opens a new chapter in Islamic education in Singapore.

milestones.description: Singapore’s emergence as a trading port in 1819 attracted Muslim merchants, scholars and settlers, fostering religious and intellectual networks.

milestones.title: Learning takes root in the community
milestones.description: Mosques, homes and teaching circles became centres of Islamic learning, supported by ulama, Sufi networks and pilgrimage connections with the wider Muslim world.

milestones.description: Singapore became a major centre of Islamic printing and publishing, producing and circulating religious texts across the Malay world.

milestones.title: Structured education expands
milestones.description: Modern madrasahs, including Al-Iqbal, Alsagoff, Aljunied and Al-Ma’arif, expanded structured Islamic education and opportunities for Muslim girls.

milestones.title: Philanthropy sustains learning
milestones.description: Muslim benefactors and community organisations sustained and expanded Islamic education through waqf, philanthropy and community initiatives.

milestones.title: Students arrive from across the region
milestones.description: Madrasahs such as Aljunied, Alsagoff and Al-Ma’arif established Singapore as a regional centre of Islamic learning, attracting students from across Southeast Asia.

milestones.title: Coordinating Islamic education
milestones.description: Institutionalisation grew from MUIS’s establishment (1968) to greater coordination through MENDAKI (1982) and the Islamic Education Advisory Board (1990).

milestones.title: Modernising full-time madrasahs
milestones.description: Curriculum reforms, national examinations, campus upgrading and MOE–NIE collaborations modernised full-time madrasah education, alongside the Joint Madrasah System (2009).

milestones.title: Learning at every stage of life
milestones.description: Community-based and lifelong Islamic education expanded through SKML, PERGAS and other providers, with structured programmes such as aLIVE, ADIL and ILHAM.

milestones.caption: Photograph of contemporary Islamic education programmes.

milestones.title: Deepening scholarly networks
milestones.description: Overseas university pathways and global intellectual exchanges through MUIS Academy, ICCOS and the Distinguished Visitors Programme deepened international Islamic education and scholarly networks.

milestones.description: Higher Islamic education and asatizah professionalisation advanced through local post-secondary institutions, accreditation, PCICS, the Syed Isa Semait Scholarship and COFA.

milestones.description: SCIS opens a new chapter in contextualised Islamic higher education, integrating Islamic scholarship, interdisciplinary research and Singapore’s socio-religious context.

closing: From early centres of learning and regional scholarly networks to modern madrasahs and institutions of higher education, Singapore’s Islamic educational tradition continues to evolve.
This heritage reflects generations of intellectual exchange, community commitment and institutional development, providing foundations for the future of Islamic education in Singapore.
opening: From the scholarly networks of a bustling port to the educational institutions of a modern nation, discover a living tradition shaped by generations of learning, exchange and renewal.
openingQuestion: What makes a place a meeting point for knowledge?

chapters.label: Connections
chapters.title: A Port of Trade. A Meeting Place of Knowledge.
chapters.intro: As Singapore developed as a trading port, it also became a meeting place for people, religious texts and ideas. Mosques, homes and teaching circles sustained learning; printing carried the written word across the Malay world.
chapters.question: What else travelled through Singapore besides goods and people?

chapters.label: Transformation
chapters.title: A Changing Society. An Evolving Education.
chapters.intro: Modern madrasahs brought structured education and new opportunities for learning. Community support, institutional coordination and curriculum reform reveal different ways of sustaining an educational tradition through changing circumstances.
chapters.question: How does an educational tradition preserve its foundations while adapting to a changing society?

chapters.label: Continuity & Renewal
chapters.title: A Living Tradition. A Shared Future.
chapters.intro: Lifelong learning and higher education extend the story beyond the classroom. The professional development of religious educators and the establishment of SCIS are contemporary chapters in a tradition that continues to evolve.
chapters.question: What does it mean to prepare religious scholars for the Singapore of tomorrow?

7.title: Institutions in a changing Singapore
7.text: The exhibition’s post-independence account follows educational coordination through MUIS (1968), MENDAKI (1982) and the Islamic Education Advisory Board (1990). These dates locate institutional development within Singapore’s changing national story.
7.basis: Dates from milestone 7. Chronological context does not establish a particular policy or causal relationship.

12.title: Scholarship in a plural society
12.text: The SCIS milestone places Islamic scholarship alongside interdisciplinary research and Singapore’s socio-religious context. It invites us to consider how an inherited intellectual tradition engages with the society in which it lives.
12.basis: Interpretation of milestone 12; SCIS is one contemporary chapter, not an inevitable endpoint.

closingReflection: Singapore’s Islamic educational heritage is a story of continuity and change. Across generations, its scholars, educators and institutions have preserved knowledge, responded to new circumstances and contributed to the life of the community.
As Singapore continues to evolve, this living tradition reminds us that heritage is not only what we inherit, but also what we carry forward.
